title: Variables
summary: Give a **value** a name so you can use it again.
refresher: A **variable** is a name that holds a **value**. You create one by assigning to it: `score = 10`. The name goes on the left, the value on the right, and the `=` means "put this value in this name". It is not a comparison. Assigning to a name that already exists replaces what was there. Using a name you never assigned is an error, because Python has nothing to look up.

blocks.body: A **variable** is a name for a **value**. You make one by assigning: put the name on the left, an equals sign in the middle, and the value on the right. From then on, writing the name means the value.

blocks.caption: Three **variables**, three types of **value**. Python works out the type on its own, so you never have to announce it.
blocks.code:
name = "Ada"
age = 36
is_student = True

print(name)
print(age)

blocks.title: The equals sign does not mean equals
blocks.body: In math, `x = 5` states a fact. In Python it gives an order: put 5 into x. That difference is why `x = x + 1` is not nonsense. It reads as "take what x is now, add one, and put the result back into x". Later, when you learn `==`, this is the distinction you will be leaning on: `=` puts a **value** in, `==` asks whether two values match.

A **variable** can be reassigned as often as you like. The new **value** replaces the old one, and the old value is simply gone. Nothing warns you, because replacing a value is usually exactly what you meant to do.

blocks.caption: Each line runs top to bottom, so the **value** you get depends on when you look. Reading `count` before the last line would have given you 1, not 2.

blocks.code:
total = 5
total = total + 3
total = total * 2
print(total)
blocks.why: Work through it one line at a time, which is exactly how Python does. `total` starts at 5. Then it becomes 5 + 3, which is 8. Then it becomes 8 * 2, which is 16. The trick is that each line uses the **value** from the line before, not the original 5.

blocks.body: Names are not arbitrary. Python has rules about which ones are allowed, and there is a strong convention about which ones you should actually pick.

blocks.title: Naming rules and habits
items: Letters, digits, and underscores only. No spaces and no dashes.
It cannot start with a digit. `score2` is fine, `2score` is not.
Case matters. `score` and `Score` are two different **variables**.
Python style is lowercase with underscores: `final_score`, not `finalScore`.
Say what it holds. `n` tells the next reader nothing; `student_count` tells them everything.

blocks.title: Using a name you never assigned
blocks.body: If you type a name Python has never seen, you get a NameError. Nine times out of ten it is a typo: you assigned `total` and then asked for `totl`. The error message names the **variable** it could not find, so read it and compare it letter by letter against where you defined it. The other cause is asking for a variable before the line that creates it has run.

blocks.caption: Python reads top to bottom. A **variable** does not exist until the assignment line has actually run, so asking for it before then is asking for something that is not there yet.
blocks.wrong:
print(greeting)
greeting = "Hi"
# asked for it one
# line too early
blocks.right:
greeting = "Hi"
print(greeting)
# created first,
# then used

blocks.prompt: Which of these lines is a **syntax error**?
choices: None of them, all four are legal
blocks.why: A name cannot start with a digit, so `1st_place` is rejected before the program even runs. `firstPlace` and `first_place2` are both legal. `firstPlace` is against Python's style convention, which prefers underscores, but style is advice and syntax is a rule. Python only refuses to run the one that breaks the rule.

blocks.body: One last habit worth starting now. When a **value** in your program has a meaning, give it a name even if you only use it once. `price * 0.06` makes a reader guess. `price * sales_tax_rate` does not.

assign-01.title: Reassignment replaces the old value
assign-01.body: A variable holds the latest value assigned to that name. A later assignment overwrites the earlier one.
assign-01.notice: Trace assignments in order from top to bottom.
assign-01.mistake: Do not add old and new values together unless the code explicitly does that.

update-01.title: The right side runs first
update-01.body: An update like `count = count + 3` reads the old value first, computes the new value, then stores it.
update-01.notice: Write the old value beside the variable before applying the update.
update-01.mistake: Do not replace both sides at the same time in your head.

swap-01.title: Copies do not preserve overwritten values
swap-01.body: Assignment copies a value at that moment. If the original value is overwritten, it is gone unless another name saved it first.
swap-01.notice: A real swap needs a temporary save or a language-specific swap pattern.
swap-01.mistake: Do not assume two assignments automatically trade values.

name-01.title: Variable names follow naming rules
name-01.body: Names can use letters, digits, and underscores, but they cannot start with a digit.
name-01.notice: Ask whether the first character is legal before checking the rest.
name-01.mistake: Do not reject underscores just because they look unusual.

undefined-01.title: Names must exist before use
undefined-01.body: The program runs in order. A name created later is not available to an earlier line.
undefined-01.notice: For runtime name errors, find the first line that tries to read the missing name.
undefined-01.mistake: Do not assume a later assignment reaches backward in time.

typein-01.title: Trace the value after every line
typein-01.body: For final-value questions, keep a small table of the variable after each update.
typein-01.notice: The printed value is whatever the variable holds at the final output line.
typein-01.mistake: Do not skip middle updates because the starting value looks simple.

compound-update-01.title: Shorthand updates still use current state
compound-update-01.body: Compound assignment means update the variable using the value it already stores.
compound-update-01.notice: Apply each shorthand operation in order and replace the stored value each time.
compound-update-01.mistake: Do not treat `+=` or `*=` as separate values waiting until the end.

copy-value-01.title: A copied value stays copied
copy-value-01.body: After one variable receives another variable's value, later reassignment of the original name does not replay old lines.
copy-value-01.notice: Assignment is an event, not a live connection for simple values.
copy-value-01.mistake: Do not update the copied variable just because the source variable changed later.

shadow-scope-01.title: Local names can hide outer names
shadow-scope-01.body: A name created inside a function or method can be separate from a name outside it.
shadow-scope-01.notice: Track which scope the code is currently running in.
shadow-scope-01.mistake: Do not assume changing an inside name changes the outside name.

static-vs-dynamic-01.title: Type rules depend on the language
static-vs-dynamic-01.body: Some languages let a name later hold a different kind of value, while typed languages require a compatible type.
static-vs-dynamic-01.notice: Read the declaration or assignment rule for the selected language before predicting behavior.
static-vs-dynamic-01.mistake: Do not transfer Python or JavaScript habits directly into Java or C++.
